title: Shared Library and Python
intro: ngspice can be built as a shared library, libngspice, that another program loads and drives: it sends netlist lines and commands, receives printed output and results through callbacks, and reads vectors directly from memory. KiCad's simulator works this way. This page shows the C interface, a complete Python example using ctypes, and the simpler alternative of running ngspice as a separate program.

items: ngSpice_Init(SendChar, SendStat, ControlledExit, SendData, SendInitData, BGThreadRunning, user): register callbacks for printed text, status messages, exit requests, per-point data and the vector list. Must be called first.
ngSpice_Circ(char lines): load a netlist from an array of lines ending with NULL (first line the title, last .end).
ngSpice_Command(\"...\"): run any control-language command: run, tran 1n 1u, alter R1 2k, bg_run (simulate in a background thread), bg_halt, bg_resume, write, quit.
ngGet_Vec_Info(\"v(out)\"): a pointer to a vector's data (name, type, real or complex values, length). ngSpice_CurPlot, ngSpice_AllPlots, ngSpice_AllVecs list what exists.

ngSpice_running, ngSpice_SetBkpt (stop a background run at a time), ngSpice_Init_Sync with GetVSRCData and GetISRCData callbacks to feed EXTERNAL sources from the program at each time point (co-simulation with a system model), ngSpice_Reset (version 44: reset completely).
Event nodes: ngGet_Evt_NodeInfo, ngSpice_Raw_Evt and ngSpice_Decode_Evt (version 45).
The header is sharedspice.h in the ngspice source and the ngspice-dev or libngspice0-dev packages.

blocks.text: This script loads libngspice, registers the callbacks it needs, loads an RC circuit, runs a transient for three resistor values and reads the time constant from the vectors. Set NGSPICE_LIB to the library's path if it is not on the default search path (libngspice.so.0 on Linux, ngspice.dll on Windows, libngspice.dylib on macOS).

It prints a time constant of 1.01, 2.01 and 4.01 ms (RC plus the sampling of the 63.2% point). The callbacks must be kept referenced (here as module-level names) for as long as the library may call them, or Python's garbage collector frees them and the program crashes. Printed output from ngspice arrives through on_char, collected in log. For long runs, bg_run starts the simulation in ngspice's own thread and BGThreadRunning reports when it ends.

items: PySpice: builds netlists from Python objects and runs ngspice through the shared library or as a subprocess; returns numpy arrays. It lags behind ngspice releases and may need its NgSpiceShared library path set for newer versions.
spicelib and PyLTSpice: run simulators as processes and read rawfiles (LTspice, ngspice, Xyce, QSPICE); good for batch sweeps and parsing results.
ngspyce and others wrap the shared library more thinly; scikit-rf reads the Touchstone files wrs2p writes.

blocks.source:
# run ngspice as a separate process, read wrdata output: no library needed
import subprocess, tempfile, os
import numpy as np

net = '''RC step
V1 in 0 PULSE(0 1 0 1n 1n 1 2)
R1 in out {r}
C1 out 0 1u
.control
  tran 10u 5m
  set wr_singlescale
  wrdata {out} v(out)
.endc
.end
'''
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    for r in ("1k", "2k"):
        cir, out = os.path.join(d, "rc.cir"), os.path.join(d, "rc.txt")
        open(cir, "w").write(net.format(r=r, out=out))
        subprocess.run(["ngspice", "-b", cir], check=True, capture_output=True)
        t, v = np.loadtxt(out, unpack=True)
        print(r, "tau =", round(t[np.argmax(v >= 0.632)] * 1e3, 2), "ms")

blocks.text: For sweeps, optimisation (scipy.optimize calling a function that writes the netlist, runs ngspice and returns a cost from meas results) and regression tests, running ngspice as a subprocess is simpler and more robust than the shared library: each run starts clean, crashes cannot take Python down, and runs parallelise with a process pool. The shared library is worth it when you need thousands of tiny runs, a live connection during a transient, or EXTERNAL sources driven by your program.

items: KiCad (eeschema): links libngspice; symbols carry Sim.* fields (model, pins, parameters), and the simulator window runs the analyses and plots the results. KiCad names nets with a leading slash (/out); when you run an exported KiCad netlist in ngspice yourself, set ngbehavior=ki so such names (and /gnd, /0 as ground in version 47) are handled.
Xschem: writes netlists with .control sections and runs ngspice on them; the usual front end with the open PDKs, whose testbenches are good starting points.
Qucs-S: a schematic editor that can use ngspice, Xyce or Qucsator, with ngspice's analyses and its own plotting.
tclspice: ngspice built with --with-tcl as a Tcl extension, for Tcl scripts and Tk front ends.

blocks.title: Two libraries
blocks.text: Your program needs two independent simulations at once. Can one process load libngspice twice?
solution: One loaded library has one global state. The manual's parallel-ngspice example copies the library under different names (ngspice1.dll, ngspice2.dll ...), loads each and initialises it with its own identification number. Simpler: run separate processes.
blocks.answer: Not as one library; load renamed copies or use separate processes.

items: H. Vogt, G. Atkinson, D. Warning and P. Nenzi, Ngspice User's Manual, version 47, 2026 (ngspice.sourceforge.io/docs.html), chapter 15 (shared ngspice and its API) and 16 (tclspice).
